headline: Kecal AI writes fake Czech chat messages to hide encrypted text
summary: This 37.5M parameter model generates casual chat to disguise AES-256-GCM ciphertext, with models downloading once and running offline in your browser.
details: Kecal is a new 37.5 million parameter open-weight language model designed to write casual Czech chat messages. It's used to power the "Chat cipher" on encrypt.click, a tool that disguises encrypted text as ordinary chat conversations, making it appear as if nothing sensitive is being shared.

The Chat cipher encrypts messages using AES-256-GCM with a key derived from a user-provided passphrase. The resulting ciphertext, along with metadata like salt and nonce, is then embedded within a generated chat conversation. This process ensures that even if the cover text is intercepted, the actual message remains secure.

The Kecal model itself, its training, the neural steganography engine, and the Czech language pack were all developed and released during the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge. The model was uploaded to Hugging Face on October 25, 2026, and integrated into encrypt.click shortly after.

For encryption and decryption, both the sender and receiver need the same model and tokenizer to ensure accurate reconstruction of the original message. The Czech model (Kecal) is 37.6 MB, while the English version (Falcon-H1-Tiny) is 93.5 MB. Both download once and operate entirely offline within the browser.

The model operates by assigning 4 bits of data to each word in the cover text, with two words representing one byte of sealed data. This deterministic approach ensures that decoding is precise. A wrong passphrase or tampered cover text will result in a failure to decrypt, rather than garbled output.

The model's licensing follows its training data: attribution, non-commercial, and share-alike. This reflects the non-permissive licensing of the corpora used for training. The model is available for download and can be run locally using ONNX Runtime Web via Hugging Face's transformers.js library.

topic: cnn outperforms frontier llms for skin cancer diagnosis
headline_marked: [[10-year-old CNN]] outperforms frontier LLMs in skin cancer diagnosis
headline: 10-year-old CNN outperforms frontier LLMs in skin cancer diagnosis
summary: A decade-old convolutional neural network, fine-tuned on dermatology images, demonstrated superior accuracy in identifying skin cancer compared to advanced AI models like GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1.
details: A dermatologist's test revealed that a 10-year-old CNN, specifically Inception v3, significantly outperformed current frontier LLMs, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, in diagnosing skin cancer from clinical and dermoscopic images. The CNN achieved a 62% accuracy rate, while the LLMs scored around 42%.

The study involved 200 biopsy-proven skin lesions, including benign growths and melanomas. When presented with both clinical and dermoscopic images, the CNN correctly identified the diagnosis for 125 lesions, whereas GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 identified 84 and 85 respectively.

The LLMs showed a tendency to over-diagnose certain conditions. GPT-6 Astra frequently misidentified melanomas as basal cell carcinoma, while Claude Fable 5.1 often classified lesions as actinic keratosis. The CNN, while not perfect, made fewer critical errors on melanoma diagnoses.

Interestingly, when asked as a patient whether a doctor's visit was necessary based on a clinical photograph alone, both LLMs advised seeing a doctor in almost every case, including for harmless lesions, highlighting a potential over-cautiousness.

The fine-tuned CNN, originally published in 2015, was trained on public dermatology image datasets and tested on lesions it had never encountered. Remarkably, this model is small enough to run in a phone browser using WebGPU, demonstrating the efficiency and capability of older, specialized AI architectures.
